'''Gideon John Davies'''  (born 6 July 1964) is a British structural biologist and chemist known for his research on the structure, mechanism, and biological roles of carbohydrate-active enzymes.<ref name=googlescholar>{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus id}}</ref><ref name=epmc>{{EuropePMC}}</ref> He is a professor at the [[University of York]] and holds the Royal Society Ken Murray Research Professorship.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2016/09/leading-scientists-awarded-royal-society-research-professorships/|title=Leading scientists awarded Royal Society Research Professorships &#124; Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref> His research work focusses on understanding how enzymes synthesise, break down, modify and interact with complex carbohydrates.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.york.ac.uk/chemistry/people/gdavies/|title=Professor Gideon Davies - Professor Gideon Davies, University of York|website=www.york.ac.uk}}</ref>

Davies’s work has contributed to the fields of [[glycobiology]], [[enzymology]] and [[structural biology]], particularly in explaining enzyme-substrate interactions and the conformational pathways involved in catalysis. His research has widespread impact, notably in [[biotechnology]] and biomedicine, and his work has also led to the development of enzyme inhibitors and probes with applications in disease research, industrial processes, and the study of the human gut microbiome.

He has received several notable honours, including the [[Davy Medal]] and the [[Gabor Medal]] of the Royal Society, and was part of the YSBL team that won the [[Queen's Anniversary Prizes|Queens Anniversary Prize]] in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.york.ac.uk/chemistry/research/ysbl/|title=York Structural Biology Laboratory - Research, University of York|first=University of|last=York|website=University of York}}</ref> He was and has been elected as a fellow of The [[Royal Society]], [[Academy of Medical Sciences (United Kingdom)|The Academy of Medical Sciences]], [[Royal Society of Chemistry|The Royal Society of Chemistry]],  and as a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization|European Molecular Biology Organization (EMBO)]]. Gideon Davies has recently been elected to the Council of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/sitecore/content/royal-society/configuration/foundation/dynamics-api/committeedetailpage/|title=Committees, Working Groups, and Councils &#124; Royal Society &#124; Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Davies grew up in [[Great Sutton]], Cheshire and attended Whitby Comprehensive School (now [[The Whitby High School]]). He went on to study at the [[University of Bristol]] where he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[Biochemistry]] in 1985 followed by a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1990 for research on the enzyme [[phosphoglycerate kinase]] isolated from the bacterium ''[[Bacillus stearothermophilus]]'', and supervised by Herman Watson and Len Hall.<ref name=phd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Gideon John|last=Davies |title=Phosphoglycerate kinase from Bacillus stearothermophilus  |publisher=University of Bristol |date=1990 |url=http://pmt-eu.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=44BU_LMS_DS000508244&vid=44BU_VU1}}</ref>  In 2007, he was awarded a [[Doctor of Science|Doctor of Science (DSc)]] degree from the [[University of Bristol]].<ref name=dsc>{{cite thesis |degree=DSc |first=Gideon John|last=Davies |title=Published work submitted for the degree of D.Sc.  |publisher=University of Bristol |date=2007 |url=http://pmt-eu.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo_library/libweb/action/display.do?doc=44BU_LMS_DS000753185&vid=44BU_VU1}}</ref>

==Career ==
Following his PhD, Davies conducted [[postdoctoral research]] at the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] (EMBL) outstation in Hamburg, where he worked with Keith S. Wilson on the use of [[synchrotron radiation]] in [[protein crystallography]]. In 1990, Davies moved to the [[University of York]] to work with Dale Wigley and [[Guy Dodson]] on the structure solution of [[DNA gyrase]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wigley |first1=Dale |title=Crystal structure of an N-terminal fragment of the DNA gyrase B protein |journal=Nature |date=1991 |volume=351 |page=624–629 |doi=10.1038/351624a0 |pmid=1646964 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/351624a0|url-access=subscription }}</ref> published in 1991.

During the early 1990s, Davies shifted his research focus to [[carbohydrate-active enzymes]], collaborating with [[Novo Nordisk]] (now [[Novozymes|Novozymes/Novonensis]]) on the structure and mechanism of cellulases — key enzymes in washing detergents and biofuels. He also spent periods as a visiting researcher at the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS) in [[Grenoble]], working with [[Bernard Henrissat]] on enzyme mechanisms, leading to the influential glycosyltransferase classification of the [[CAZy]] database.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/S0959-440X(97)80072-3 | title = Structural and sequence-based classification of glycoside hydrolases | journal = Current Opinion in Structural Biology | volume = 7 | issue = 5 | pages = 637–644 | year = 1997 | last1 = Henrissat | first1 = B. | last2 = Davies | first2 = G. | pmid=9345621}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/S0969-2126(01)00220-9 | title = Structures and mechanisms of glycosyl hydrolases | journal = Structure | volume = 3 | issue = 9 | pages = 853–859 | year = 1995 | last1 = Davies | first1 = G. | last2 = Henrissat | first2 = B. | pmid=8535779 | doi-access = free}}</ref> He also collaborated with [[Alwyn Jones (biophysicist)|Alwyn Jones]] on computer graphics applications and in studying plant polysaccharide-degrading enzymes.

In 1996, Davies was awarded a [[Royal Society University Research Fellowship]], which allowed him to establish his own research group within the [[York Structural Biology Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/gideon-davies-6769/ |title=Gideon Davies |website=royalsociety.org |language=en-gb |access-date=2017-06-14 |archive-date=28 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180628044106/https://royalsociety.org/people/gideon-davies-6769/ |url-status=dead}}</ref> He was promoted to professor at the University of York in 2001 and was awarded a Royal Society Ken Murray Research Professorship in 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2016/09/leading-scientists-awarded-royal-society-research-professorships/ |title=Leading scientists awarded Royal Society Research Professorships |website=royalsociety.org |language=en-gb |access-date=2017-06-14}}</ref>

In 2000, Davies was the inaugural Peter Wall Catalytic Visitor at the [[University of British Columbia]], where he collaborated with [[Steve Withers]] and [[David Vocadlo]] on the structural and mechanistic analysis of hen egg white lysozyme.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Vocadlo |first1=David |title=Catalysis by hen egg-white lysozyme proceeds via a covalent intermediate |journal=Nature |date=2001 |volume=412 |pages=835–838 |doi=10.1038/35090602 |pmid=11518970 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/35090602}}</ref>

Davies was elected a member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] in 2010 and is a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (FRSC). In 2010, he was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS). His Royal Society citation states: {{centered pull quote|''Professor Gideon Davies' research is focused on "structural enzymology". In this he addresses the enzymes, and their [[protein domain|accessory domains]], that are involved in the synthesis, modification and breakdown of carbohydrates. His chemical and structural insight into [[Protein–carbohydrate interactions|protein-carbohydrate interactions]] and his brilliant exploitation of advanced crystallographic methods provide the basis for understanding how the chemical and structural factors in the [[stereochemistry|stereochemical]] pathway of the [[Enzyme substrate (biology)|enzyme:substrate complex]] govern specificity and catalysis. His research is having an immense impact on carbohydrate chemistry and biology and biological catalysis generally''.<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2010/gideon-davies/ |title=Professor Gideon John Davies FRS |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=2015-11-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151123143239/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2010/gideon-davies/ |location=London |url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

In 2014, Davies was elected a Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences. His citation notes: {{centered pull quote|''Gideon Davies, who is Professor of Biological Chemistry at University of York, has made world-leading contributions to Biochemistry. He has made fundamental additions to our understanding of enzyme mechanism and carbohydrate biochemistry. As a direct result of his work into the conformation of sugars during turnover, he described the [[rational design]] of [[Enzyme inhibitor|highly potent inhibitors]] of [[O-linked glycosylation|O-linked glucosamine modifying enzymes]]. These compounds are showing potential as treatments for [[Alzheimer's disease]]. Recently he has turned to study the human [[Microbiome|microbiota]], which are now recognised to be an essential component of human health, and their carbohydrate [[metabolism]] is implicated in several disease states''.<ref name=fmedsci>{{cite web |url=http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-gideon-davies/ |title=Professor Gideon Davies FRS FMedSci |publisher=The Academy of Medical Sciences |archive-date=2014-10-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141026212044/http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-gideon-davies/ |location=London |url-status=dead}}</ref>}}

Davies also serves on the scientific advisory board of Alectos Therapeutics, a private pharmaceutical company focusing on the discovery and development of therapeutics for neurological diseases.

===Former group members===

Several of Davies' former students and postdoctoral researchers have advanced to prominent roles in academia and industry. Notably, [[Tracey Gloster]] is a professor at the University of St Andrews, recognized for her work on carbohydrate-processing enzymes. [[David Vocadlo]] is a professor at Simon Fraser University, holding a Canada Research Chair in Chemical Glycobiology and co-founding Alectos Therapeutics. David Zechel serves as a professor at Queen's University, focusing on enzyme mechanisms and natural product biosynthesis.

===Research===

Davies' research focuses on the biological chemistry of carbohydrates, combining structural biology, enzymology, and glycobiology to understand how carbohydrate-active enzymes function at the molecular level. His group has used advanced techniques such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy to study glycoside hydrolases, glycosyltransferases, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases (LPMOs), and polysaccharide lyases — enzymes critical for biomass degradation, cell wall remodelling, and microbial interactions.

A major focus of Davies' research has been dissecting the structures and catalytic mechanisms of enzymes central to industrial biotechnology, particularly those involved in the degradation of complex polysaccharides such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and starch. By solving the crystal structures of cellulases, xylanases, lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases, and industrial enzymes such as the bacterial α-amylases, his group has provided detailed molecular insights that have informed the design of improved enzyme formulations for applications in biofuel production, biomass conversion, and detergents.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brzozowski |first1=A.M. |title=Structural origins of the catalytic power and substrate specificity of a bacterial α-amylase |journal=Biochemistry |volume=39 |pages=9099–9107 |year=2000 |doi=10.1021/bi0000317}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{Cite journal |last1=Quinlan |first1=R.J. |title=Insights into the oxidative degradation of cellulose by a copper metalloenzyme that exploits biomass components |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=108 |pages=15079–15084 |year=2011 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1105776108|pmc=3174640 }}</ref> His work has thus contributed directly to advancing sustainable industrial processes and bio-based technologies.

His work on glycoside hydrolase mechanisms has provided key insights into substrate distortion, transition states, and conformational pathways, shaping the understanding of enzymatic catalysis and informing the design of selective enzyme inhibitors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ducros |first1=V.M.A. |title=Substrate distortion by a beta-mannanase: snapshots of the Michaelis and covalent-intermediate complexes suggest a B(2,5) conformation for the transition state |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |volume=41 |issue=15 |pages=2824–2827 |year=2002 |doi=10.1002/1521-3773(20020802)41:15<2824::AID-ANIE2824>3.0.CO;2-G |pmid=12203498}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tailford |first1=L.E. |title=Structural and biochemical evidence for a boat-like transition state in beta-mannosidases |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=4 |pages=306–312 |year=2008 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.81}}</ref>

Davies has made major contributions to the discovery and characterization of LPMOs, revealing their role in oxidative polysaccharide degradation and opening new routes for industrial biotechnology applications.<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hemsworth |first1=G.R. |title=Discovery and characterization of a new family of lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=10 |pages=122–126 |year=2014 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.1417|pmc=4274766 }}</ref>

Davies has extensively investigated the enzyme O-GlcNAcase (OGA), which regulates the dynamic post-translational modification of proteins by O-linked N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc). His structural and mechanistic studies on bacterial and human OGAs and OGTs<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Meek |first1=Richard |title=Cryo-EM structure provides insights into the dimer arrangement of the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine transferase OGT |journal=Nature Communications |date=2021 |volume=12 |page=6508 |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-26796-6  |doi-access=free|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-26796-6|pmc=8586251 }}</ref> have provided critical insights into substrate recognition, catalysis, and inhibitor design.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dennis |first1=R.J. |title=Structure and mechanism of a bacterial β-glucosaminidase having O-GlcNAcase activity |journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology |volume=13 |pages=365–371 |year=2006 |doi=10.1038/nsmb1079}} </ref> These discoveries have laid the foundation for the development of OGA inhibitors as potential therapeutic agents targeting neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Alzheimer’s disease, where abnormal tau phosphorylation plays a critical role.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yuzwa |first1=S.A. |title=A potent mechanism-inspired O-GlcNAcase inhibitor that blocks phosphorylation of tau in vivo |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=4 |pages=483–490 |year=2008 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.96}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roth |first1=C. |title=Structural and functional insight into human O-GlcNAcase |journal=Nature Chemical Biology |volume=13 |pages=610–612 |year=2017 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.2358|pmc=5438047 }}</ref>

Davies' work on glycosyltransferases has significantly advanced understanding of the enzymatic mechanisms underlying glycosylation, a process essential for modifying small molecules, lipids, and proteins. His structural studies have elucidated how human, plant and bacterial glycosyltransferases recognize substrates and catalyze the transfer of sugar moieties, with applications ranging from antibiotic biosynthesis to xenobiotic detoxification.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Offen |first1=W. |title=Structure of a flavonoid glucosyltransferase reveals the basis for plant natural product modification |journal=The EMBO Journal |volume=25 |pages=1396–1405 |year=2006 |doi=10.1038/sj.emboj.7600970|pmc=1422153 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bolam |first1=D.N. |title=The crystal structure of two macrolide glycosyltransferases provides a blueprint for host cell antibiotic immunity |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=104 |pages=5336–5341 |year=2007 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0607897104|pmc=1838483 }}</ref> His work has provided molecular blueprints for engineering glycosyltransferases with altered specificity or enhanced activity, broadening their biotechnological and pharmaceutical applications.

His research has been funded by the [[Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council]] (BBSRC), the [[European Research Council]] (ERC), and [[Alzheimer's Research UK]]. Davies has published over 400 papers in peer-reviewed journals.<ref name=googlescholar/><ref name=scopus/><ref name=epmc/>

===Awards and honours===
Davies has been recognized with numerous national and international awards for his groundbreaking research in carbohydrate enzymology, structural biology, and biotechnology.  

He was awarded the [[Davy Medal]] (2015) by the [[Royal Society]], one of its premier medals for outstanding contributions to chemistry, recognizing his pioneering structural studies on carbohydrate-active enzymes. He received the [[Gabor Medal]] (2010) for interdisciplinary work combining biology and chemistry, notably his insights into enzyme mechanisms and applications in biotechnology.  

He is also the recipient of the John and Rita Cornforth Award of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 2020,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/archives/rita-and-john-cornforth-award/|title=Rita and John Cornforth Award|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> (jointly with Paul Walton), acknowledging exceptional collaborative research. Other major honours include the Royal Society of Chemistry's Haworth Memorial Lectureship,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/membership-and-community/connect-with-others/through-interests/interest-groups/carbohydrate-group/haworth-memorial/|title=Haworth Memorial Lectureship - a Carbohydrate Group Award|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> the Khorana Prize for outstanding contributions through work at the chemistry and life science interface<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/find-a-prize/chemistry-biology-interface-division-open-award-khorana-prize/|title=Chemistry Biology Interface open prize: Khorana Prize|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> the [[Corday–Morgan Medal and Prize]] and the RSC's Dextra Carbohydrate Chemistry Award, highlighting his contributions to chemical biology and enzymology.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/membership-and-community/connect-with-others/through-interests/interest-groups/carbohydrate-group/dextra-carbohydrate-chemistry-award/|title=Dextra Carbohydrate Chemistry Award - a Carbohydrate Group Award|website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref>

Internationally, Davies shared (with Paul Walton and Bernard Henrissat) the [[IChemE]] [[Global Awards#Global Energy Award|Global Energy Award]] (2016) for industrial biotechnology innovation leading to biofuels, and the Whistler Award of the International Carbohydrate Organization for his lifelong contributions to carbohydrate science.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ico.chemistry.unimelb.edu.au/whistler-award/|title=Roy L Whistler International Award in Carbohydrate Chemistry – International Carbohydrate Organisation}}</ref> In 2026 he was awarded the [[Bruce_A._Stone]] [https://www.cazypedia.org/index.php/B.A.%20Stone%20Award%20for%20Excellence%20in%20Plant%20Polysaccharide%20Biochemistry Award] for Excellence in Plant Polysaccharide Biochemistry. 

In 2019, the York Structural Biology Laboratory team, including Davies, was awarded the [[Queen's Anniversary Prizes|Queen's Anniversary Prize]], the highest national honour for UK higher education institutions, for its outstanding research in protein science leading to new drugs, therapies, and improved industrial processes.

==Personal life==
Davies married Valérie Marie-Andrée Ducros in 1999 (div. 2021) and has two daughters.<ref name=whoswho/>
